name: Qaqet
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Tabain, Marija & Birgit Hellwig. 2022 [print issue 2023]. Qaqet (Illustration of the IPA). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 53(3): 1073-1094. doi:10.1017/S0025100321000359 (open access, CC-BY; Cambridge Core PDF held).
catalog_locator: Section 'Stress', p. 1087; Figure 10 p. 1088; intonation remarks p. 1089
catalog_quote: Qaqet does not have lexical stress. There are no minimal pairs, and there is no evidence for the existence of metrically strong syllables as anchor points for post-lexical pitch accents. Figure 10 shows syllable duration, mean f0 and mean RMS energy, for words varying from one to six syllables in length. ... It can be seen that there is no effect of syllable position on mean f0 (although there is generally greater variability in f0 on the final syllable of the word, most likely due to the fact that the data are taken from word-list recordings). Similarly, there is no effect of syllable position on mean RMS energy (although there may be a tendency for some initial and final syllables to have less energy). By contrast, there is a clear effect of syllable position on duration. It can be seen that, broadly speaking, final lengthening extends over the last (two-to-)three syllables of the word. ... This suggests differential effects of phrase-final lengthening on consonants and vowels. ... Preliminary analyses suggest that this final lengthening is accompanied by intonational phenomena which mark the right edge of prosodic units. Hellwig (2019: 52-63) presents a preliminary inventory of such pitch movements ... The other spectrogram examples in this Illustration highlight the generally flat f0 contours on the prosodic words in the language, with only microprosodic variation due to consonant.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No lexical (word) stress: no stress minimal pairs and no metrically strong syllables serving as anchors for pitch accents; f0 and intensity do not vary by syllable position; the only positional effect is durational final lengthening over the last two to three syllables of the word (in word-list citation forms), accompanied by intonational pitch movements at the right edge of prosodic units. This reinterprets the older SIL impression (Parker & Parker 1974: 34; OPD 2004) that non-contrastive, variable 'stress' tends to fall on the final two syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None; source denies metrical structure altogether.
new_statements.exceptions: Phonemic schwa does not show final lengthening (citing Hellwig 2019); greater f0 variability on word-final syllables attributed to word-list recording context; possible tendency for some initial and final syllables to have less energy. Parker & Parker 1974 (Kakat dialect) instead report a tendency for stress on the final two syllables, varying between elicitations, with disyllables stressed on both syllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Measurements are on words from word-list recordings (citation forms), 620 lexical items / 4221 syllables from six female speakers of Raunsepna village; the durational effect is explicitly treated as phrase-/unit-final lengthening tied to right-edge intonation (Hellwig 2019: 52-63), not word-level prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Tabain & Hellwig 2022 (and Hellwig 2019) describe Qaqet as spoken in Raunsepna village (mountainous interior of the Gazelle Peninsula); Parker & Parker 1974 and the 2004 SIL OPD describe the 'Kakat dialect' of 'Baining' from Walmetki (west coast) and Ialam — same language (qaqe1238, ISO byx; Kakat = Qaqet), different localities. Glottolog lists no sub-dialect codes for Qaqet. Not to be confused with Mali Baining (mali1284) or Ura (urab1240), which have separate phonologies (Stebbins 2011; Stanton 2007).

sources.citation: Parker, Jim & Diana Parker. 1974. A tentative phonology of Baining (Kakat dialect). In Richard Loving (ed.), Phonologies of four Papua New Guinea languages (Workpapers in Papua New Guinea Languages 4), 5-43. Ukarumpa: Summer Institute of Linguistics.
sources.note: Image-only scan (SIL REAP copy via the Internet Archive); scanned pp. 32-35. Sec. 5.3 Stress, p. 34: 'No contrastive stress pairs have been found. Stress in elicited words tends to vary from one occasion to another. The tendency is for words to have stress on the final two syllables. Hence words of two syllables have stress on both syllables.' Examples ['la:p'ki] 'cockatoo', [ma'lep'ka] 'ten', [ga'lep'ki] 'axe handle'. Sec. 5.2 p. 33: utterance-finally, stress produces lengthened final consonants. Fieldwork Walmetki village (west coast), checked with Ialam speakers, 1971-72.
sources.venue: Phonologies of four Papua New Guinea languages

sources.citation: Tabain, Marija & Birgit Hellwig. 2022 [print issue 2023]. Qaqet (Illustration of the IPA). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 53(3): 1073-1094. doi:10.1017/S0025100321000359. Open access (CC-BY).
sources.note: Section 'Stress', p. 1087: 'Qaqet does not have lexical stress. There are no minimal pairs, and there is no evidence for the existence of metrically strong syllables as anchor points for post-lexical pitch accents.' Instrumental data (620 lexical items, 4221 syllables, Fig. 10): no effect of syllable position on f0 or RMS energy; clear final lengthening over the last (two-to-)three syllables of the word, accompanied by right-edge intonational pitch movements (refers to Hellwig 2019: 52-63). Data recorded in Raunsepna village.
sources.venue: Journal of the International Phonetic Association

sources.note: No word-stress statement. Ch. 6 'Prosodic features' treats CDS f0 range/mean and speaking rate; p. 108 cites Hellwig (2019: 56) that Qaqet intonation units have a flat contour with all major pitch movements at the right boundary; utterance ends are prosodically prominent. Defers to Hellwig 2019 for linguistic analysis.

tone.summary: No tone system stated. Prosody as reported (secondhand from Hellwig): pitch movements confined to intonation-unit boundaries with an inventory of eight boundary contours; no lexical stress. Lexical tone is not mentioned at all.
